content_html:
This calculator estimates what college will cost by the time your child enrolls, how much your current savings plan will have built up by then, and the monthly amount that would cover the full bill. It uses your own cost figure rather than a national average, because prices vary widely between community colleges, public universities and private schools, and the number that matters is the one for the schools your child is likely to attend.

How to use this calculator

  1. Annual college cost in today's dollars: one year of tuition, fees, housing and food at today's prices. A school's net price calculator, which every college that takes federal student aid must publish on its website, gives an estimate after typical grants.
  2. Years until college and years of study: for a 6-year-old who will start at 18, enter 12. Use 4 for a bachelor's degree or 2 for an associate degree.
  3. College cost inflation: how quickly you expect prices to rise each year. College costs have often risen faster than general inflation, so testing a higher and a lower rate is sensible.
  4. Current savings and monthly contribution: what you have set aside today, for example in a 529 plan, and what you add each month.
  5. Expected annual return: an assumed average return on those savings. A cautious figure is safer for money you'll need on a fixed date.
  6. Share of costs to pay from savings (under More options): lower it if you expect scholarships, grants, your income at the time or student loans to pay part of the bill.

How the projection works

Each year of college is priced separately. The first year's cost is today's cost grown by the inflation rate for the number of years until enrollment, and each later year is one more year of inflation on top. Your savings grow with monthly compounding and an end-of-month contribution until the first semester. From then on contributions stop, each year's bill is paid at the start of the year and whatever is left keeps earning the same return.

The monthly saving needed is found by discounting all the college bills back to the enrollment date, subtracting what your current savings will have grown to, and spreading the remainder over the months you have left. Saving exactly that amount leaves a zero balance after the last bill is paid.

A worked example

Suppose one year at the school you have in mind costs $25,000 today, college starts in 12 years and lasts 4, costs rise 5% a year, you have $10,000 saved, you add $300 a month and you expect a 6% return.

  • The first year will cost about $44,896, and all four years together about $193,509.
  • Your savings will reach about $83,553 when college starts, enough for the first year and part of the second.
  • The projected shortfall is about $107,572, so the plan covers roughly 44% of the cost.
  • Saving about $743 a month instead of $300 would cover all four years.

Change the share of costs to 50% and the monthly figure drops sharply, which shows how much difference expected aid or a contribution from current income makes.

Practical tips

  • Start early: with 12 years to go most of the final balance can come from growth, while with 4 years to go nearly all of it has to come from contributions.
  • 529 plans let savings grow free of federal income tax when the money is used for qualified education expenses, and many states add a deduction or credit for contributions.
  • Re-run the numbers each year with the latest prices and your actual balance, and move toward safer investments as enrollment approaches.
  • Paying for part of the cost is a reasonable goal. Many families combine savings, current income, aid and modest borrowing.

The results are estimates based on constant rates. Actual costs, investment returns and financial aid will differ, and the figures are before any taxes or fees.

faq.question: How much should I save for college each month?
faq.answer: It depends on the expected cost, the years remaining and how much of the bill you plan to cover from savings. Enter your own figures and the calculator shows the monthly amount that would pay the full projected cost, or the share you choose.

faq.question: What college cost inflation rate should I use?
faq.answer: There is no single correct figure. Published price increases have varied a lot from year to year and between public and private schools, so try two or three rates, for example 3%, 5% and 7%, and plan around a middle result.

faq.question: Should I include room and board in the annual cost?
faq.answer: Include whatever you expect to pay for from savings. If your child will live at home, use tuition and fees plus books and transportation; if they will live on campus, add housing and meal plan costs.

faq.question: What happens to the savings while my child is in college?
faq.answer: The calculator stops monthly contributions at enrollment, pays each year's bill at the start of that year and lets the remaining balance keep earning the same return until it is needed.

faq.question: Does the calculator account for financial aid or taxes?
faq.answer: Not directly. To allow for grants, scholarships or loans, lower the share of costs paid from savings under More options. Results are before any taxes or account fees.
